sourceNotes: Seeded from QSRM roleplay performance indicators and hospitality and tourism cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: QSRM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the hospitality and tourism cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The timed segment the lane's detection loops actually measure — order point to product handout — which deliberately excludes the minutes a car spends queued before it reaches the order point.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judge asks why guests complain about a five-minute wait when the store posts a 175-second average; the answer is that the standard measures only the segment after the order point.

terms.definition: The full clock a vehicle is in the lane, from triggering the entry loop to clearing the window, so it carries the queue the service-time standard leaves out: a store averaging 180 seconds of service with six cars stacked ahead at 30 seconds apiece is delivering a 360-second experience.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case gives both a service-time average and a queue length, the exam answer is that only total experience time explains falling satisfaction scores at a store hitting its speed target.

terms.definition: Cars sent to a waiting bay before their food is handed out, divided by cars served — the figure that tells you how much of a posted speed number is real, because the lane timer stops when the car leaves the window even though the order is still open. At 20% pull-forward with a two-minute average bay wait, true handout time runs about 24 seconds longer than the board says.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the district manager asks why a store leads the market on timers but trails on accuracy and complaints is solved by pulling the pull-forward rate.

terms.definition: The ceiling a lane can serve in an hour, found by dividing 3,600 seconds by the cycle time of the slowest station rather than by the average order time — a 40-second grill cycle caps the lane at 90 cars an hour no matter how fast the window and order taker are.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a peak-hour forecast of 110 cars, the exam expects you to compare it against this ceiling and conclude the store will lose cars unless the constraining station is relieved.

terms.definition: The longest per-order processing time among the positions in the line, which alone sets what the whole store can produce — cutting ten seconds at a 25-second assembly position while the 40-second fry station is untouched changes hourly output by zero, and relieving the fry station simply moves the constraint to whatever is now slowest.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that hands you station-by-station timings and one extra crew member is testing whether you deploy that person to the constraint instead of the busiest-looking spot.

terms.definition: The alternation rule that decides how orders from two side-by-side order points are sequenced into one production line and one window — commonly one-for-one, or weighted toward the outside lane. Two order points add roughly 10 to 15 percent throughput only while the ratio is enforced; unmanaged merging makes orders arrive out of sequence and the re-sorting at the window gives the gain back.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on a store that added a second order lane and saw no throughput improvement is asking about merge discipline, not equipment.

terms.definition: How many cars can queue on the property before the line spills into the street or blocks the parking lot, judged against the queue the peak actually creates: serving 90 cars an hour with a four-minute average wait means six cars are in line at any moment, so an eight-space stack works and a five-space stack sends the ninth car away.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and remodel roleplays turn on this number, because a lane that blocks a public road can put the store in violation of its use permit.

terms.definition: Vehicles that enter the lane or lot and leave without ordering, divided by vehicles that entered — sales that never appear in any sales report, which is why the loss is invisible without lane counters. One point of it during a 120-car hour at a $9 average check is more than $10 an hour of sales gone.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to justify a second order point or a bump in peak staffing, you quantify the case with drive-offs rather than with complaints.

terms.definition: The seconds a guest genuinely spends facing the board — roughly 20 to 40 in a moving drive-thru lane against 60 to 90 at a counter — which caps how many rotating creative frames anyone actually sees. Four frames on a 15-second rotation is a 60-second loop, so a 25-second dwell shows under two of them and a promotion parked in frame four reaches almost nobody.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay asking why a limited-time offer under-sold despite full digital-board coverage is testing whether you check rotation length against dwell.

terms.definition: The number of minutes ahead of a guest's predicted arrival that an order-ahead app releases the ticket to the kitchen, computed from GPS travel time minus cook time. Release too early and the food sits toward the end of its hold window; release too late and the guest waits at a pickup shelf — a seven-minute ETA on a three-minute build means holding the ticket about four minutes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on cold or stale order-ahead pickups is answered by tuning this offset, not by adding crew.

terms.definition: The seconds between an order appearing on a station's screen and the crew member clearing it, logged per station and per ticket. Comparing the same tickets across stations tells you which position is actually accumulating the delay, so the number decides where the next labor hour goes instead of leaving it to whoever looks busiest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table of station timings in a case, the expected answer identifies the constraining station from bump times rather than from total order time.

terms.definition: The maximum minutes a cooked item may stay in the holding cabinet before quality standards require discarding it, and therefore the hard cap on cooking ahead: with a 20-minute standard, you may only pre-cook what the forecast says sells in the next 20 minutes, so an item selling 15 an hour supports a staged batch of five.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask you to raise speed without raising waste are decided by batching inside this window, and a judge will expect the arithmetic, not the promise.

terms.definition: The table that converts the next half hour's forecast into how many finished units should be sitting in the cabinet right now — target level equals forecast sales across one hold window plus a small buffer, minus what is already held. It replaces cooking by feel, and it is why two managers with the same forecast stage the same amount.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on preparing for a bus rush or a school lunch surge wants the build-to arithmetic, since cooking to a guess produces either a queue or a bin of discards.

terms.definition: The staged quantity of each prepped component held at the assembly line when a daypart opens, set as forecast usage over the restock interval plus a buffer — 30 minutes of usage if a runner restocks every half hour. Set it high and prepped product ages out of standard; set it low and the line stops mid-peak to refill.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay on a line that keeps stalling during lunch is solved by recalculating pars against the restock interval, and the judge is listening for that interval.

terms.definition: The seconds equipment needs to return to its cooking setpoint after a frozen load drops in, which belongs in the station's true cycle: a three-minute cook plus 45 seconds of recovery is a 3:45 cycle, so a four-vat battery yields about 64 baskets an hour rather than the 80 the cook time alone suggests.
terms.whyItMatters: Capacity questions that ask whether existing equipment can carry a forecast peak are wrong by 20 percent if you plan on cook time and ignore recovery.

terms.definition: Units cooked and then discarded divided by units cooked, read against the projection that ordered them — the direct price of staging ahead for speed. Thirty discards on a 1,000-unit day is three percent, and a rate near zero is usually evidence of under-projecting and making guests wait rather than of good discipline.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay pairing a speed complaint with a waste complaint expects you to treat the two as one tradeoff and name the rate you would accept.

terms.definition: Net sales divided by every crew and management hour worked in the same period — $4,800 across 120 hours is $40 — giving a productivity figure that does not move when the wage rate moves, unlike labor cost as a percentage of sales, which improves on paper the moment menu prices rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to defend a schedule to a franchisee watching labor percentage, you argue in this measure because it separates crew productivity from pricing and wage changes.

terms.definition: Guest transactions divided by crew hours worked, which unlike its dollar-denominated sibling is immune to menu price increases — so when the dollar measure climbs eight percent after a price rise while this one is flat, the store gained pricing, not productivity.
terms.whyItMatters: A case showing improving labor metrics after a price increase is testing whether you can tell a real efficiency gain from an arithmetic one.

terms.definition: The grid that turns each hour's forecast sales into a crew count and a named position for every person on the floor — one added crew member per roughly $150 of incremental hourly sales, with the added position specified. It is what makes two managers with the same forecast schedule the same people to the same stations.
terms.whyItMatters: A scheduling roleplay gives you a sales forecast by hour and expects a staffed schedule out of it, not a headcount guess.

terms.definition: Scheduling one crew member for two separated blocks in a single day so they cover both the lunch and dinner peaks without being paid through the slow afternoon between them. Several jurisdictions require a premium payment when the unpaid gap exceeds a set length, so the savings are not automatic.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on cutting labor without cutting peak coverage points here, and the judge expects you to flag the premium rule rather than assume the hours are free.

terms.definition: Net sales divided by the number of transactions, not by the number of people fed — a single drive-thru transaction may carry four meals — so it rises with party size, combo mix and upsize rate as readily as it does with price.
terms.whyItMatters: A case reporting a rising average check with flat transactions expects you to identify which of those drivers moved before crediting a price increase.

terms.definition: The share of eligible orders sold in the larger size, and the highest-leverage number on the order taker's scorecard because the incremental cost of a bigger drink or fry is pennies: 100 upsizes a day at a $0.70 upcharge against $0.10 of added cost drops about $60 a day straight to contribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a selling roleplay to raise sales without raising traffic or prices, you quantify the opportunity from this rate and the upcharge spread.

terms.definition: Entrée transactions sold as a bundled meal rather than à la carte, divided by entrée transactions — each point moves the average check by the bundle premium, so lifting 55 percent to 60 percent across 400 daily entrées is 20 more combos a day and the premium multiplied by that.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion or coaching roleplay that must produce a dollar projection is built from this rate, the entrée count and the bundle premium.

terms.definition: The percentage of an order subtotal a marketplace platform retains for listing, dispatch and courier pay — commonly 15 to 30 percent depending on the tier bought. A $20 order at 30 percent nets $14, which turns an item earning a healthy in-store margin into a loss delivered unless price, basket size or tier changes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on whether to join or stay on a delivery marketplace is decided by running this rate against the item margins, not by counting incremental orders.

terms.definition: The percentage by which listed prices are raised on a marketplace to leave the same dollars behind after commission — and the raise is not equal to the commission. Covering a 30 percent take requires dividing by 0.70, a 42.9 percent increase; matching it at 30 percent still leaves the store nine percent short.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing question on delivery menus is graded on this reciprocal, and matching the commission percentage is the trap answer.

terms.definition: The transaction count a block of the day must hit for its contribution to cover the labor and fixed cost of being open for it: $260 of scheduled breakfast labor against $2.60 of contribution per transaction breaks even at 100 transactions, and averaging 70 means opening early loses money every morning.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on whether to open earlier, close later or drop late night is settled with this arithmetic rather than with traffic counts.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: A court's decision to set aside limited liability and reach the owners' personal assets, available when the entity was run as a mere alter ego: personal and business funds commingled, formalities ignored, the firm deliberately undercapitalized at formation, or the corporate form used to work a fraud. Ordinary business failure never suffices — the owner has to have treated the corporation as a pocketbook.
terms.whyItMatters: Ownership-structure roleplays ask what an entrepreneur must actually do after incorporating to keep a house and savings out of reach.

terms.definition: A five-step persuasive outline - attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action - where the fourth step is the one that distinguishes it: the audience is walked through a vivid picture of life after adopting the proposal (or of life if they refuse) before any request is made. A plain problem-solution outline stops after satisfaction, and a call to action without the visualization step is the most common way competitors flatten it back into three parts.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks you to sell a manager on a new procedure, this sequence gives a scored structure; naming the five steps beats an unstructured pitch every time.

terms.definition: An organization-wide commitment to continuous improvement and quality.
terms.whyItMatters: A quality culture lowers defects and lifts loyalty over time.

terms.definition: An inquiry the sales team has formally accepted after confirming a named need, a budget owner and a decision timeline, where a marketing-qualified lead has cleared only a behavior score such as downloads or page visits. Handoff agreements usually give sales a fixed window, often 24 hours, to accept it or send it back with a stated reason.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel items ask at which stage marketing's responsibility ends and sales' begins; a roleplay on fixing a marketing-sales dispute is scored on defining the acceptance criteria and the return window.

terms.definition: The European rule granting individuals rights of access, correction, portability and erasure over their own data, requiring a documented lawful basis before any processing begins, forcing breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours, and capping fines at the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: An international e-commerce roleplay asks what changes when the site starts shipping to Ireland, and the answer is these specific obligations and their clock, not a general promise of privacy.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: Maps five ways of handling a disagreement — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating — on two axes: assertiveness, meaning concern for your own outcome, and cooperativeness, meaning concern for the other party's. Collaborating is high on both and costs the most time; compromising sits at the middle of both and splits the difference, so treating those two as synonyms is the classic wrong answer.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict roleplays name a deadline, and the judge wants the mode matched to it — collaborate when the relationship and the outcome both matter and time exists, compromise when it does not.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: The percentage of a covered cost the policyholder keeps paying after the deductible is met, such as 20% of every bill until an out-of-pocket maximum is reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Health-plan comparison items test that meeting the deductible does not end the client's share of the bill.

terms.definition: A formal document in standard format used for official outside communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect correct formatting, tone, and structure.

terms.definition: A physical or software constraint that makes the wrong action impossible or immediately obvious — a plug that only fits one way, a field that refuses an invalid date — so defects are PREVENTED at the source, unlike statistical process control, which detects defects after they have already been produced.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method questions distinguish prevention from detection, and the mistake-proofing device is the accepted example of prevention when a scenario describes a repeated human error.

terms.definition: A model where reps sell entirely by phone, email and video from one location, never traveling to the customer. A field visit costs roughly five to ten times as much per contact, so firms set a deal-size floor — accounts below it are covered from the desk and only larger ones earn a visit, which is a coverage-cost decision rather than a preference.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items give a cost per contact and an average order size and ask which channel serves an account segment; a territory-planning roleplay is graded on justifying coverage by cost, not by habit.

terms.definition: Standards governing the responsible collection, use, protection, and sharing of information.
terms.whyItMatters: Privacy and data-governance dilemmas are common in modern business scenarios.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: Non-wage offerings such as health insurance, retirement plans, and paid time off.
terms.whyItMatters: Benefits influence hiring decisions and employee satisfaction.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: Written 30-, 60- or 90-day document listing measurable targets, the support the employer will provide and the stated consequence of missing them. It is not progressive discipline's verbal-then-written-warning ladder: discipline addresses conduct the employee chose, this addresses capability, and it doubles as the documentation trail for a for-cause termination.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervision roleplay about an employee who is trying hard and still missing quota calls for this, while a no-call-no-show calls for the discipline ladder instead.

terms.definition: An argument broken into six named parts: the claim, the grounds (the data offered), the warrant - the usually unstated assumption that licenses moving from the grounds to the claim - plus backing that supports the warrant, a qualifier that limits how strongly the claim holds, and a rebuttal that names the conditions under which it fails. Arguments collapse at the warrant far more often than at the data, because the missing piece was never said aloud.
terms.whyItMatters: Defending a recommendation to a judge who pushes back means naming the assumption connecting your figures to your conclusion, which is the step competitors skip when they simply repeat the data louder.

terms.definition: A Pareto split of stock by annual dollar usage: roughly the top 20 percent of items carrying about 80 percent of the value are class A and get tight control and frequent counts, class B moderate control, class C the low-value bulk that is managed loosely with large buffers.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a warehouse manager should spend limited counting and control effort, the accepted answer is to classify by dollar usage and concentrate on class A rather than treat every item alike.

terms.definition: The one person who controls the funds and can release them without another signature, distinct from a technical buyer who screens against specifications and can veto but never approve, and from a user buyer who judges daily impact and lives with the result. Only one of the three can say yes; either of the other two can end the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe three contacts and ask who must be reached before the close; an organizational-selling roleplay is graded on identifying who signs rather than pitching whoever answered the phone.

terms.definition: Copies only the blocks changed since the previous backup of any type, so each nightly run is the smallest possible, but restoring requires the last full backup plus every one of these runs applied in order since it — and a single missing or corrupt link breaks the entire chain behind it.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-storage items ask why a company whose nightly job finishes in four minutes still needed nine hours to recover, and the restore chain is the reason.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: A defect-reduction discipline targeting no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities, executed through the DMAIC sequence — define, measure, analyze, improve, control — with trained belt roles owning each project; it attacks process variation, while lean methods attack waste and cycle time.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations-management exam items name the improvement sequence and expect the letters of DMAIC in order along with the defect target.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: A specific financial or market goal that pricing decisions aim to achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives, like profit or market share, guide pricing recommendations.

terms.definition: Tufte's distortion metric: the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data, where an honest chart lands between 0.95 and 1.05. A 20 percent rise drawn as a bar twice as tall scores 5; scaling a pictogram by both height and width doubles a doubling into a fourfold area, scoring about 2. A truncated vertical axis inflates it the same way, which is why a bar chart's axis must start at zero even when a line chart's need not.
terms.whyItMatters: Data-visualization items give a chart and ask why it misleads, and the scored answer names the exaggeration, not just 'the graph looks unfair.'

terms.definition: A doctrine holding that one bottleneck sets the output of the whole system, worked through five focusing steps — identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it with added capacity, then repeat because the constraint has moved — so improvement anywhere else adds inventory, not throughput.
terms.whyItMatters: When a production roleplay describes one slow station, the judge wants the constraint named and the rest of the line paced to it, not a blanket speed-up of every station.

terms.definition: An insider with real political capital who argues the vendor's case in meetings the vendor is not invited to, and whose own standing rises if the purchase works out. A coach, by contrast, supplies intelligence and coaching on how to navigate the account but cannot spend influence or move the decision — access is not the same as power.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe a friendly contact who shares information but has no budget and ask what role that person plays; a long-cycle selling roleplay expects you to test for personal stake, not just friendliness.

terms.definition: Copies everything changed since the last full backup, so Friday's run is far larger than Monday's, but a restore needs exactly two pieces — the full backup plus the newest run — against the incremental approach's full backup plus every intervening night in sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-continuity roleplay trades nightly window against recovery speed, and the graded answer is which of these two schemes buys the shorter restore.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: The default American rule that either side may end the relationship at any time for any reason or none, narrowed by three recognized exceptions: a public-policy exception covering firing for jury service, refusing to break the law, or whistleblowing; an implied-contract exception built from handbook language or long practice; and, in a minority of states, an implied covenant of good faith. Statutes on race, sex, age, disability and retaliation override it outright.
terms.whyItMatters: Termination roleplays ask what a manager may put in a handbook without accidentally promising contractual job security.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: Divides what is known about a person into four panes by crossing known-to-self against known-to-others: open, blind, hidden and unknown. Asking for feedback shrinks the blind pane, while voluntary self-disclosure shrinks the hidden pane — the two moves are not interchangeable, and only the first can surface a habit you cannot see in yourself.
terms.whyItMatters: A written item asking which pane a manager reduces by running a 360-degree review, and roleplays that ask a competitor to assess personal strengths and weaknesses, both depend on separating feedback from disclosure.

terms.definition: Interference produced by the message's own words - unfamiliar jargon, an ambiguous pronoun, a term whose connotation differs for sender and receiver - as opposed to physical noise, which is external to the message (a loud room, a dropped call, small type), and psychological noise, which is inside the receiver (anxiety, distraction, a prior grudge). The distinction decides the fix: repeating the sentence louder cures only the physical kind.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam scenario where a customer misreads a policy term is a semantic-noise item, and the scored remedy is rewording, not resending.

terms.definition: Scheduling deliveries to arrive as production consumes them so carrying cost and warehouse space approach zero; the explicit trade against safety-stock buffering is that it removes the cushion that absorbs a late supplier, so one disrupted shipment stops the line.
terms.whyItMatters: A supply-disruption roleplay wants both halves — the carrying-cost saving and the exposure it creates — because recommending it without naming the supplier-reliability requirement is what costs the point.

terms.definition: Helping customers make purchase decisions through planned communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling vocabulary supports recommendations about staff, service, and revenue.

terms.definition: The mathematical examination of data to identify patterns, test relationships, and support decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are tested on interpreting findings and drawing evidence-based conclusions.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: The amount a policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance pays anything, and the lever that moves premiums — a higher one lowers the monthly cost and raises the risk carried.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-selection scenarios ask which policy suits a client, and the answer depends on whether they could absorb that first payment in an emergency.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: The differential between a long-tenured employee and a newly hired peer shrinking to nothing or inverting — a five-year employee at $58,000 next to a new hire brought in at $61,000 because market rates rose faster than annual merit increases of 3%. It differs from a straight pay-equity gap in that the cause is market movement over time rather than a protected characteristic, and the fix is a market adjustment, not a discrimination remedy.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay in which top performers resign after a hiring spree is usually a compression problem, and naming the differential is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Visual tools such as charts and diagrams that reinforce a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must select and justify aids that support their analysis.

terms.definition: Available production time in a shift divided by customer units demanded in that shift — the pace demand dictates, which is set outside the factory, unlike cycle time, the pace the line actually achieves; a cycle time above it means the plant cannot keep up with orders.
terms.whyItMatters: Line-balancing items give shift minutes and a daily order quantity and ask how often a unit must come off the line; confusing the demand-set pace with the observed one flips the answer.

terms.definition: Deals won divided by every qualified opportunity worked in the period — 15 wins out of 60 qualified opportunities is 25%. The denominator keeps opportunities that are still open or that ended in no decision, which is exactly what win rate throws out, so this figure always reads lower than win rate for the same rep.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales-management roleplay that asks you to diagnose a rep whose revenue is falling, a dropping close rate against a steady win rate points at unqualified prospecting rather than weak closing technique.

terms.definition: A 99.999% uptime commitment, which permits roughly 5.3 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year; each nine dropped multiplies that allowance by ten, so 99.99% permits about 53 minutes, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, and 99% about 3.65 days — which is why a vendor's extra decimal costs so much.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay compares two hosting quotes whose uptime promises differ by one decimal, and converting each into annual minutes is what makes the price gap defensible.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: Seven-factor analysis the Department of Labor applies to decide whether an unpaid intern is really an employee: who gains the greater benefit, whether the work is tied to academic credit, whether it displaces paid staff, and whether either side expects a paid job at the end. If the employer is the main beneficiary, minimum wage and overtime are owed retroactively.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay staffing a startup with unpaid interns is scored on this test, because failing it turns free labor into back wages.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: A growth grid crossing products (existing vs. new) with markets (existing vs. new) to produce four moves — market penetration, market development, product development, and diversification — ordered from lowest to highest risk because each new axis adds unfamiliar variables.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks how a regional chain should grow next year is answered by naming the specific Ansoff cell and its risk level, not by saying 'expand'.

terms.definition: Edward Hall's study of how people use physical distance, mapped to four zones: intimate from contact to about 18 inches, personal from 18 inches to 4 feet, social from 4 to 12 feet, and public beyond 12 feet. Normal business is transacted in the social zone, so a salesperson who closes to 3 feet has entered personal space and is read as pressure rather than warmth. The distances themselves are cultural, and the same 3 feet reads as ordinary in much of Latin America and as intrusive in northern Europe.
terms.whyItMatters: Nonverbal-cue items describe a customer stepping back during a demonstration, and the scored answer names the zone violation instead of calling it 'being uncomfortable.'

terms.definition: Availability multiplied by performance multiplied by quality, each a percentage — so a machine running 90 percent uptime at 90 percent of rated speed with 90 percent good output scores about 73 percent, which is why the product exposes losses the three separate rates hide.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment and maintenance questions ask why a line reported as 'ninety percent up' still misses its quota; multiplying the three loss categories is the accepted way to show it.

terms.definition: The structured steps that move a customer from awareness to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the process helps competitors execute each stage well.

terms.definition: A cloud arrangement where the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualization while the customer still patches the operating system and everything stacked above it; platform services shift that operating system and runtime to the provider, and software as a service leaves the customer responsible for nothing but their own data and user settings.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks who is at fault when an unpatched server is breached, and the answer depends entirely on which of these three lines the contract drew.

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: Compares unit sales to buyers' income rather than to price: %change in quantity / %change in income. A positive coefficient marks a normal good and a value above 1 marks a luxury, while a negative coefficient marks an inferior good whose sales rise when incomes fall.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions about which line a retailer should push in a downturn are decided by the sign of this figure, not by the product's margin.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: A federal tax election under Subchapter S that keeps corporate limited liability while passing profit and loss straight through to the owners' personal returns, escaping the double taxation a C corporation pays once at the entity level and again on dividends. The price is eligibility: no more than 100 shareholders, only individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents, and a single class of stock.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-ownership exam items ask which form a startup taking on 120 investors or a foreign backer can no longer use.

terms.definition: Albert Mehrabian's finding that when a speaker's words, tone and facial expression contradict each other about how they feel, listeners resolve the conflict by weighting words 7 percent, tone of voice 38 percent, and facial expression 55 percent. The routine misuse is the claim that 93 percent of all communication is nonverbal: the studies tested single words about liking, said by women, in a laboratory, and say nothing about the content of an informational message. Cited correctly, it covers incongruence only.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the standard trap answer on nonverbal-communication items, and a judge who has heard the '93 percent' line all day notices the competitor who states its actual scope.

terms.definition: Continuous small improvements generated by the workers doing the job, accumulating gradually at near-zero capital cost — deliberately opposed to kaikaku or reengineering, which is a rare, top-down, capital-heavy redesign of the whole process.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how to streamline work without a budget, the incremental frontline approach is the fitting recommendation, and the judge listens for why you did not propose a full redesign.

terms.definition: Deals won divided only by the deals that reached a final decision — wins plus losses — so 15 wins among 45 resolved deals is 33%, with open and no-decision opportunities excluded from the denominator entirely. That narrower denominator is the whole difference from close rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that hand you a pipeline table expect you to notice which opportunities belong in the denominator; counting still-open deals as losses is the single most common wrong answer.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: Techniques to address disagreements and reach mutually acceptable solutions.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong conflict resolution keeps teams cohesive and prevents escalation.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring lenders to disclose the annual percentage rate, finance charge and total payments in a standard form before a consumer signs.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why two loan offers in a roleplay can be compared at all, and why a lender quoting only a monthly payment is out of compliance.

terms.definition: Presenting numbers and trends visually so patterns are clear.
terms.whyItMatters: Visuals make recommendations look credible and actionable.

terms.definition: Software that explodes a master production schedule through the bill of materials and nets it against on-hand stock to time component orders; it plans materials only, while enterprise resource planning extends the same database to finance, human resources and sales as one system.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology-in-operations items test whether you can scope the two acronyms apart — the narrow materials planner versus the company-wide platform — which is the discrimination most competitors get backwards.

terms.definition: Identifying and qualifying potential customers who may need an offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective prospecting builds the foundation for successful sales.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: Including people of different backgrounds, perspectives, and identities in the workforce.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversity improves problem-solving and reflects the customer base.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: Minimum number of members who must be present for a body's votes to count — a majority of the membership under Robert's Rules unless the bylaws set something lower, often one third. Business conducted without one is void rather than merely defeated, so a motion that loses 3 to 2 stands as rejected while the same motion passed short of this number stands as nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A chapter-officer or board roleplay in which half the members skip the meeting is scored on whether the competitor recognizes that no decision can be made.

terms.definition: The nonverbal channel of body motion - posture, gesture, facial expression and eye behavior - which is distinct from paralanguage, the vocal qualities wrapped around the words (pitch, rate, volume, pauses, filled hesitations like 'um'), and from chronemics, the messages carried by the use of time such as arriving late, answering after three days, or scheduling only 10 minutes. Naming the right channel matters because each has a different repair.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask you to read a supervisor's crossed arms, clipped tone and delayed reply are testing three separate channels in one scenario.

terms.definition: A five-step workplace discipline — sort out what is not needed, set remaining items in fixed marked locations, shine and inspect, standardize the arrangement in writing, and sustain it by audit — where the fifth step is the one that fails and turns the program into a one-time cleanup.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety and efficiency roleplays reward naming a structured method for a cluttered work area rather than saying 'organize it,' and the sustain-by-audit step is the detail that separates a full answer.

terms.definition: Open opportunity value divided by the quota for the period: $900,000 of open deals against a $300,000 quota is 3x, the usual rule of thumb for a team that wins about one deal in three. Coverage below the reciprocal of the win rate means the quota is arithmetically unreachable no matter how well the rep sells.
terms.whyItMatters: A district-manager roleplay judged on forecasting expects you to test coverage before promising a number, and to prescribe prospecting rather than closing coaching when coverage is thin.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: An industry-attractiveness framework scoring five pressures — rivalry among existing firms, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer bargaining power, and supplier bargaining power — where high scores on several forces predict compressed industry margins; it maps the industry, not the single firm, which is what separates it from a SWOT.
terms.whyItMatters: Management roleplays that ask you to brief an owner on whether to enter a crowded category are scored on naming and applying all five pressures, not on listing generic pros and cons.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: The knife-edge case where the coefficient equals exactly 1: a 10% price cut brings a 10% volume gain and total revenue does not move at all. Above 1 demand is elastic and revenue moves opposite to price; below 1 it is inelastic and revenue moves with price.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a matched pair of percentages and ask what happens to revenue, and recognizing this case rather than assuming revenue rises is the trap being tested.

terms.definition: The parliamentary manual whose thresholds get tested: a main motion needs a second and passes on a simple majority of votes cast, an amendment needs a majority, closing debate by moving the previous question needs two-thirds because it takes away a member's right to speak, and a tie fails. Precedence governs order - while an amendment is pending, no new main motion is in order - and a point of order can interrupt because it concerns the rules rather than the question.
terms.whyItMatters: Officer and staff-meeting scenarios ask what vote a motion requires, and the two-thirds threshold for cutting off debate is the one competitors miss.

terms.definition: A dependency network that estimates each task's expected duration as optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic, divided by six — a weighted three-point estimate for work with uncertain durations, unlike a critical path calculation, which assumes one fixed duration per task.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you three time estimates for a task and ask for the expected duration; the weighted formula, not a plain average of the three numbers, is the scored answer.

terms.definition: The opening contact and strategy used to engage a potential customer.
terms.whyItMatters: A professional approach sets the first impression that drives interest.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: Reaches single-firm conduct and requires two elements: monopoly power in a properly defined relevant market, and the willful acquisition or maintenance of that power through exclusionary conduct rather than growth from a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident. Section 1 instead needs an agreement between two or more parties restraining trade, so one firm acting alone can violate Section 2 and never Section 1.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-issues exam items about a dominant platform cutting off rivals turn on which section of the Act is even available.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation until the required feeling is genuinely experienced, so expression and emotion match — as against surface acting, where a smile is layered over an unchanged feeling. The two produce the same visible behavior with opposite costs, because it is the mismatch inside surface acting, not the effort of acting, that drives exhaustion.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching roleplays where a supervisor must help a frustrated employee face the public are graded on teaching the employee to reframe the customer's motive rather than just ordering a better face.

terms.definition: A structured idea session run in four fixed stages: members write ideas silently and independently, then a round-robin in which each person contributes one idea per turn with no discussion allowed, then clarification of each posted item, then private ranking whose tally decides the outcome. Silent generation and one-at-a-time posting are what separate it from open brainstorming, where the loudest member anchors the room; the Delphi technique goes further by keeping experts anonymous across written rounds so they never meet at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Problem-solving group items ask which method protects the quiet member's idea, and this is the process that names how.

terms.definition: A horizontal bar timeline showing each task's start, duration and overlap against calendar dates; it displays schedule but not logic, whereas a PERT network draws the dependency arrows that reveal which tasks actually control the finish date.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-management roleplays ask which tool to bring to a status meeting: the bar timeline communicates progress to a client, but it cannot answer which delay pushes the deadline.

terms.definition: Number of open opportunities multiplied by average deal size multiplied by win rate, all divided by the average sales cycle length in days, which yields revenue per day: 50 x $4,000 x 0.30 / 60 days = $1,000 a day. It is the one common metric where shortening the cycle raises revenue without adding a single new prospect.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks which of four fixes lifts revenue fastest, the velocity formula shows that cutting cycle time is a divisor change and beats a small win-rate gain.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: A deposit locked for a fixed term at a fixed rate, paying more than a savings account in exchange for a penalty on early withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-vehicle scenarios rule it out for an emergency fund precisely because the money is not reachable without giving up interest.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
