terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: A grid whose rows are performance ratings and whose columns are quartiles of the pay range, with a percentage in each cell: an outstanding performer in the first quartile might receive 6% while the same rating in the fourth quartile receives 3%, and a below-standard rating receives 0% anywhere. The two-way design keeps high performers moving toward the midpoint while stopping anyone from being pushed past the maximum.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a rating and a compa-ratio in a roleplay, you are expected to read the correct cell and explain why two people with the same rating get different percentages.

terms.definition: Standard structures for business documents such as memos, reports, and proposals.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the correct format for each document type.

terms.definition: Summing durations along every dependency chain and taking the longest one as the shortest possible project duration; every task on it has zero float, so any slip there slips the whole project, while a delay off it is absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A project roleplay that asks which of several late tasks to escalate is answered by locating the zero-float chain, because effort spent on the others buys no finish-date improvement.

terms.definition: Asking questions to understand a customer's problems, goals, and requirements.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing needs ensures recommendations truly solve the customer's problem.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: How a product or brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning shapes differentiation and appeal to the target market.

terms.definition: Senior advocate who spends political capital on someone's behalf in rooms that person is not in, putting their name into promotion and staffing decisions and absorbing reputational risk if it goes badly. A mentor spends time instead of capital — advice given directly to you, with nothing of the mentor's own staked on the outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on advancement patterns is scored on this distinction, because the competitor who only asks for coffee chats never gets named in the promotion meeting.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: A Kaplan-and-Norton performance system that reports four linked perspectives — financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth — so that lagging money measures are read alongside the leading operational drivers that produce them, unlike a plain profit-and-loss review.
terms.whyItMatters: Management written events ask how a manager tracks strategy beyond revenue; naming all four perspectives and one measure inside each is what earns the points.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 index of how far a society's less powerful members accept unequal distribution of authority - Malaysia scores near 100, Austria near 11, the United States around 40. It is a separate dimension from individualism: a high-power-distance audience expects the most senior person to speak first, treats public disagreement with a manager as an attack, and takes an invitation to challenge the presenter as a trap, so a presentation that works in a low-index room must be restructured rather than merely translated.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to adapt a pitch for an overseas client, the scored answer changes who presents and how questions are invited, not just the language.

terms.definition: A deliverable-oriented decomposition of a project into progressively smaller work packages governed by the 100 percent rule — the children of any element must sum to exactly that element, no more and no less — so it captures scope, not sequence, which the schedule adds afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how to start planning a project, the accepted first move is decomposing deliverables before estimating or scheduling, and the completeness rule is what stops forgotten work becoming a budget overrun.

terms.definition: Units of a specific add-on sold divided by units of the primary product sold, times 100 — 300 protection plans on 1,000 phones is 30%. It scores one named pairing, where cross-sell measurement counts every additional category a customer buys, so a store can raise total cross-sell revenue while this figure falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays that set an accessories goal are graded on whether you name the ratio you will move and the counter behavior that moves it, not on a general promise to sell more.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: Two towns pull trade from the countryside between them in proportion to their populations and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to each; the indifference line sits at the miles between them ÷ (1 + the square root of the larger town's population divided by the smaller town's), measured out from the smaller town, and households past that line shop the larger one.
terms.whyItMatters: A trading-area item on the marketing exam gives two populations and the miles between the towns and expects the boundary mileage as a number; in a site-selection roleplay it is how you defend where a store stops drawing customers instead of waving at a map.

terms.definition: The price a manufacturer recommends retailers charge for a product.
terms.whyItMatters: MSRP frames legal and ethical pricing and channel relationships.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: Blocks a merger or acquisition whose effect may be substantially to lessen competition — an incipiency standard reaching a deal before any harm has occurred, unlike the Sherman Act, which needs a completed restraint or actual monopolization. Deals above reporting thresholds must be cleared with the FTC and DOJ before closing, and the agencies may sue to enjoin, force divestiture, or accept behavioral conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Merger roleplays ask why regulators can stop a deal that has not yet raised a single price for a single customer.

terms.definition: A readability formula that grades a passage as 0.4 x (words per sentence + percentage of words carrying three or more syllables), so it counts only 'hard words' instead of weighting every syllable the way Flesch-Kincaid does. On the same paragraph the two scores diverge whenever long sentences are built from plain words: a 40-word sentence of one-syllable words drives fog up sharply while Flesch-Kincaid barely moves. General business writing is normally targeted at 12 or below and news writing near 11.
terms.whyItMatters: An editing item hands you one paragraph and two readability scores and asks which formula flagged it, and a roleplay defending a rewritten warranty is scored on naming a target number rather than promising the draft now 'reads better.'

terms.definition: Latest allowable start minus earliest possible start for a task — the delay it can absorb before the project finish moves; total float is shared along a chain, whereas free float is the smaller amount that delays no immediately following task at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a network with early and late start dates, exam questions ask how long a task can slip; confusing the shared allowance with the task-level one over-promises the client in a status roleplay.

terms.definition: A product's characteristics and the value those characteristics give.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must separate features from benefits to sell effectively.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: Estimates the probability a shopper in a neighborhood picks one particular store as that store's selling area ÷ travel time raised to a decay exponent (commonly 2), divided by the same ratio summed across every competing store; multiplying that probability by neighborhood households and their annual category spending turns it into a sales forecast for the site.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-comparison questions that ask which of three locations captures the most volume are solved by ranking size-over-distance-squared ratios, and unlike a single breaking-point line this one gives every store a share of every neighborhood — the distinction a judge probes.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation before the emotion peaks so that the feeling itself changes — an antecedent-focused move, as opposed to expressive suppression, which lets the feeling run and hides only the outward signal. Suppression is the costlier of the pair: it consumes attention, degrades memory of the conversation, and leaves internal arousal untouched.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking which self-control tactic preserves a manager's recall of a hostile meeting expects reappraisal, and roleplays on composure reward reframing over a clenched poker face.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: Federal law governing consumer credit files: it grants access to the report, sets who may pull it, and obliges a bureau to investigate a disputed item.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in a roleplay whose report shows an account they never opened has a statutory remedy under it, not just a complaint.

terms.definition: The medium — email, phone, in person, memo — chosen for a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Justifying channel choice signals professional maturity.

terms.definition: Comparing budgeted cost of work actually completed against what was spent and what was planned: cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost, schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and any index below 1.0 signals over budget or behind schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-evaluation items ask whether a project that has spent sixty percent of its budget is in trouble; only the ratio against work completed answers it, and a raw spending percentage does not.

terms.definition: A six-part qualification framework — Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion — that adds the buyer's internal mechanics, the written criteria and the approval path, to the money-and-authority checks BANT stops at. It is built for long committee purchases where the signer is never the first contact.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business roleplay with a committee, naming the economic buyer and the decision criteria is the specific step judges look for before any presentation content.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: A distinctive strength that lets a business outperform its competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Naming the advantage shapes marketing messages and differentiation.

terms.definition: Employer benefit and payroll-tax cost expressed as a percentage of base pay — $19,500 of insurance, retirement and taxes on a $65,000 salary is a 30% load, making the fully loaded cost $84,500. National figures put benefits near 31% of total compensation, which is why an offer decision compares loaded cost rather than salary alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Budgeting a new position in a roleplay is wrong if you quote only the salary; judges look for the loaded figure when the owner asks what the hire really costs.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: Prompt demanding a specific past incident, on the premise that past behavior predicts future behavior, with answers scored against written anchors — which is why a hypothetical answer earns zero. A situational question does the opposite, asking what you would do in a scenario you have never faced, and is scored for reasoning rather than evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: The interview portion of a job-seeking roleplay is graded on giving a dated, quantified incident when the question asks for one, not a description of your general habits.

terms.definition: Scores a passage from 0 to 100 where a HIGHER number means easier, running opposite in direction to every grade-level formula: 206.835 - 1.015 x (words per sentence) - 84.6 x (syllables per word). The 60-to-70 band is the plain-English range consumer documents target, 30 and below is college-graduate difficulty, and 90-100 is fifth-grade text. Because the scale runs to 100, a score of 70 is good here while a grade-level score of 70 would be absurd.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items and written-event judges both hand you a score and ask whether the document suits its audience; reading this 0-to-100 scale as though it were a grade level reverses your answer.

terms.definition: Inspecting a randomly drawn sample from a delivered lot and accepting or rejecting the entire lot on the count of defects found, against a stated acceptable quality level — the highest defect percentage treated as satisfactory — which trades a known risk of passing a bad lot for the cost of inspecting every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Receiving-process questions ask how a buyer verifies a large shipment economically; naming the tolerable defect percentage and the risk it accepts is what distinguishes a full answer from 'check some of them'.

terms.definition: A method built on teach, tailor and take control, in which the rep opens with a commercial insight that reframes how the buyer sees their own business and then respectfully pushes back on the buyer's assumptions. Relationship selling does the reverse: it builds trust first and delivers whatever the buyer already says they want.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judged on demonstrating expertise rewards teaching the buyer something about their own market, while a purely agreeable rep reads as an order taker.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: Weights availability by the share of category dollar volume rung up in the stores that stock an item rather than the share of stores stocking it: 400 supermarkets out of 2,000 can be 65% ACV when they are the busiest 400, so an item in a fifth of outlets can still stand in front of two-thirds of category purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution items hand a store count alongside a volume weighting and expect the weighted figure; a marketing-plan roleplay that claims 'we reach most of the market' collapses when the judge asks which of the two numbers that claim rests on.

terms.definition: A two-by-two positioning model crossing source of advantage (low cost vs. differentiation) with competitive scope (broad market vs. narrow niche), yielding cost leadership, differentiation, and focus; a firm that lands in the middle of the grid is 'stuck in the middle' and holds neither advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a firm's cost and pricing profile and ask which generic position it occupies, so the two axes have to be named separately rather than answered as 'it competes on quality'.

terms.definition: Puts a written or drawn description of an unbuilt product before target buyers and scores stated purchase intent, normally reading the top two boxes of a 5-point scale -- 'definitely' plus 'probably would buy' -- then discounting that figure, because stated intent runs far above actual trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Feasibility roleplays ask how you would test an idea before building it; naming the intent scale and the discount separates a real answer from 'ask some customers.'

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: Infers elasticity from the direction revenue moves after a price change: if raising price raises total revenue, demand is inelastic; if revenue falls, demand is elastic; if revenue holds steady, elasticity is unitary. It needs no coefficient at all, unlike the midpoint calculation it substitutes for.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges accept this shortcut when a candidate has to justify a price increase on the spot without the data to compute an elasticity coefficient.

terms.definition: Letter layout that keeps the inside address, salutation, body paragraphs and any lists flush at the left margin but starts the dateline, complimentary close and signature block at the horizontal center of the page - about the 3-inch tab on a page with 1-inch margins. That one shifted column is the only difference from full block; adding a half-inch first-line indent to every paragraph converts it again into semi-block.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting questions show the same letter three ways and score the competitor who can point to which elements moved, rather than judging the page by how balanced it looks.

terms.definition: Charting sample measurements over time against limits computed from the process's own variation to separate common-cause noise from assignable-cause shifts; it monitors a process while it runs, unlike acceptance sampling, which judges a finished lot after the fact.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method roleplays ask how to catch a drifting machine before it produces scrap; watching the charted trend is the in-process answer, and inspecting finished goods is the one judges mark as too late.

terms.definition: Connecting a product feature to the benefit the customer receives.
terms.whyItMatters: It turns product facts into customer value.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: Counts the plain percentage of outlets in the defined universe that stock an item — 400 of 2,000 stores is 20% — and says nothing about how much those outlets sell; dividing weighted (%ACV) coverage by this number gives a quality-of-distribution ratio that runs above 1.0 when the item sits in the bigger stores and below it when the item is stranded in small ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-choice questions supply both coverage figures and ask which distribution plan is stronger; the ratio between them is the answer, and treating the two numbers as interchangeable is the classic miss on that item.

terms.definition: The classification system that assigns every imported article a code — six digits harmonized worldwide, extended to ten digits in the United States — and it is that code, not the invoice description, which sets the duty rate and any quota or trade-remedy exposure. Misclassification remains the importer's liability even when a customs broker filed the entry, so back duties and negligence penalties land on the buyer.
terms.whyItMatters: Customs-regulation roleplays ask why two nearly identical shirts arrive carrying very different duty rates.

terms.definition: Laws and rules ensuring fair practices and safeguarding customer rights.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding it helps a business operate ethically and avoid liability.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth builds organic advocacy and trust beyond paid ads.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: The ability to discuss and reach agreements that satisfy multiple parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation determines outcomes in sales, contracts, and partnerships.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' pole opposite universalism: which rule applies depends on the relationship and the circumstance, so a signed contract is a starting point a long-standing partner may reopen, and an obligation to a friend can outrank written policy. Universalist cultures - the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany - hold that one standard binds everyone regardless of who is asking, which is why the identical request reads as reasonable flexibility on one side of the table and as favoritism on the other.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay where a long-time distributor asks for terms no other account receives is scored on naming the cultural logic at work before ruling on the request.

terms.definition: Unloading inbound freight and transferring it directly to outbound trailers within hours, sorting by destination on the dock, so the goods are never put away — the opposite of conventional warehousing, which stores, picks and holds stock and therefore incurs carrying cost that this eliminates.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about cutting inventory cost and speeding delivery expect this as the named technique, and the judge wants the requirement that inbound and outbound schedules be tightly synchronized.
